body:
## Module 1 in two minutes

Two studies appear to contradict each other and don't. SHRM's mapping of AI across HR practice areas puts **employee relations among the least-adopted areas in the function.** HR Acuity asked ER teams what they had actually done: **70% experimented with or deployed AI for ER and investigations in 2025**, and **only 56% restrict it to approved, secured tools for confidential case content.**

Both are sound. One asked organizations about institutional adoption; the other asked practitioners about behaviour. So:

> **Institutionally this is the least AI-adopted part of HR. Behaviourally, seven in ten ER teams have already used it. The gap is unsanctioned use, in the most confidential documents your organization produces.**

The sample, because this module is about evidence: 274 US organizations of 1,000+ employees, 8.8 million employees, ±5.9 points, fielded early 2026 on 2025 practice. **It says nothing about employers under a thousand people.**

And the reason, which matters more than the reproach: serious misconduct allegations have **more than doubled since 2021** while ER staffing moved 0.6 → 0.68 per 1,000. **Unsanctioned use is arithmetic, not indiscipline**, and a prohibition nobody can comply with produces **concealment**, which is worse: same exposure, no record, no way to know which files were affected.

### The evidentiary ladder

Five rungs. Every piece of work product in this function sits on exactly one.

**1 · Observation**: what was said, seen, recorded. *"The complainant states that…"*
**2 · Corroboration**: what other evidence exists, supports, contradicts, or is **missing**.
**3 · Inference** — what it could mean, held plural. *"Three readings are available…"*
**4 · Finding**: what you conclude happened, to a standard. **Requires weighing.**
**5 · Determination**, what follows for a named person.

AI may organize and transcribe at rung one. At rung two it may **locate what exists, what conflicts, and what is missing** — the most valuable rung, and fully permitted. At rung three it may generate **untested plural possibilities** and never rank or select one. **At rungs four and five, nothing.**

> **The rung boundary, not the task, is the control.**

That formulation is the point. *"AI may help with summaries"* is unusable, a summary can sit on any rung, and the same request produces rung-two output on Monday and rung-four output on Tuesday. **"AI may establish what exists and may not weigh it" is a rule you can apply to a sentence.**

And note the frame isn't primarily a restriction. **Rung two is where cases are won and lost**: the missing statement, the unrequested document, the uninterviewed witness. It tells you where the leverage is.

**The full module applies the ladder to the automation you'll be sold first: intake triage.** It is high-volume, rules-shaped, and it decides **whether a matter gets investigated at all**, which makes it a **rung-five determination wearing rung-one clothing.**

The reason it's the worst place for it: accelerating someone through a process is visible and recoverable; filtering someone out is invisible. **The person whose complaint was downgraded never appears in your substantiation data**, so the failure mode is structurally unmeasurable. And unlike a candidate who never learns they were filtered, **this person had a right to be heard and knows they raised something.** Your metrics show a healthy function; their experience is that nothing happened. 38% of organizations have no required investigation process that would catch it.

So: **AI may extract and structure what an intake contains**: allegations, dates, parties, whether retaliation or a protected characteristic is mentioned. **It may not decide severity, priority, or whether to investigate.** And whatever you decide, **track downgraded matters as a category, with a reason and a named decider, and sample them** — not to second-guess every call, but to find out whether the pattern of "no" has a shape.

One last thing the module insists on: **every control has to be cheaper than the workaround**, or it loses to the workaround.
